title: The Mixed-Methods Advantage
intro: Running a mixed-methods study and being a mixed-methods researcher are different things.

learn.title: What the second one means
learn.text:
A mixed-methods researcher can **work in either tradition**, **connect findings from studies never designed to combine**, and **interpret single-method data more carefully**.

Example: interviews weeks ago showed a confusing CTA label; today's analytics show a drop at that step. Nobody planned that connection — noticing it is the skill.

try.q: What can a mixed-methods researcher do that a specialist often can't?
options: Connect studies that weren't designed to combine
try.explain: Plus working in either tradition and reading single-method data more carefully.

learn.title: Three ways to mix by design
learn.text:
**1. Measure, then investigate** — analytics find the drop-off; interviews explain it.
**2. Investigate, then measure** — usability finds a problem; a first-click test sizes it.
**3. Together** — completion rates and interviews on the same tasks.

What makes it mixed methods is **planning both methods and their integration before the study** — not which one comes first.

try.q: What makes a study genuinely mixed methods?
options: Using qual and quant in one project
Reporting both in the same deck
Having both a researcher and an analyst
try.explain: Order doesn't matter; planned integration does.

learn.title: Why it's a career argument
learn.text:
As research teams shrink, Calabro argues **qual-only is no longer a safe career strategy**.

This is also where his own view evolved: in 2023 he was calling for *more qual* in analytics-heavy teams. By 2025–26 the position is integration — neither tradition alone.

try.q: How did Calabro's position change between 2023 and 2026?
try.explain: The 2023 article argued for more qualitative work; the later ones argue for mixing.

test.q: What does quantitative data typically not tell you?
test.explain: Patterns and magnitude, but rarely the reason.

test.q: What does qualitative data typically not tell you?
test.explain: It finds unexpected problems without sizing them.

test.q: In “investigate, then measure”, what comes second?
options: A study that sizes the problem
test.explain: For example a first-click test after usability testing finds the issue.

test.q: What does a mixed-methods mindset change when only one method is used?
options: You interpret the single source more carefully
You always add a second method
You report lower confidence by default
test.explain: The habit applies even to single-method work.

test.q: Why does team size matter to this argument?
options: Smaller teams need researchers who cover both
test.explain: As teams shrink, breadth becomes a safety issue.
